analysis.one_liner: Requires a judge's warrant before government agencies can obtain Americans' phone and internet records.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Judiciary Committee and a subcommittee until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023, with only one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, federal and state agencies can use an administrative subpoena — paperwork signed inside the agency, not by a judge — to force email, phone, and cloud providers to hand over customer records, including the metadata showing who you contacted, when, and from where. This bill would amend the Stored Communications Act so that a judge would have to issue a warrant, based on the criminal standard, before any of those records could be disclosed. It would apply going forward but would not unwind disclosures already made.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone with a phone, email account, or cloud storage — effectively everyone — gains a shield against warrantless government access to the records of their communications. Under the bill, police and federal agents could no longer obtain a person's contact records, location information, and usage history with an internal subpoena; a judge would have to find probable cause first.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone with a phone or email

how_it_helps.text: Requires a warrant issued by a court before a government entity can obtain a customer's records, including metadata, from a phone, email, or cloud provider, closing the administrative-subpoena path that currently exists for records other than communication contents [S2][S3].

Extends the warrant requirement to stored communications regardless of how long they have been stored, by removing the 180-day rule that let older stored emails be obtained through a subpoena rather than a warrant [S3].
Bars future expansions of prior disclosures: any request to broaden or follow up on a record disclosure made before enactment would have to meet the new warrant standard [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement agencies lose the fastest tool for obtaining contact and location records: an internal subpoena. Investigations that today proceed in days could require a judge's sign-off. Communications providers see little change, since they already respond to warrants for message contents; their main new burden is that a slightly broader category of requests must go through the warrant process.

drawbacks.text: The bill strikes the exceptions paragraph of the records-disclosure statute, which today permits non-warrant disclosures in emergencies, with customer consent, and through other legal processes; removing it could slow or block time-sensitive law enforcement requests, such as locating a missing person [S3].
The change applies only to future requests; records already turned over before enactment stay disclosed, and any harm from past warrantless access is not remedied [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but narrow: the public gains a judge's check on a routine surveillance power, while investigators lose speed and, under the bill as written, the emergency and consent exceptions for records. A more careful version would have preserved emergency carve-outs. On balance the bill moved privacy law toward the standard most people assume already applies — that the government needs a warrant to see their records — and its main flaw was drafting breadth, not its goal.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, sent to its crime subcommittee about six months later, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Lieu introduced the bill on April 21, 2022, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S5].
On November 1, 2022, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, and no further action was recorded before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].
The bill drew a single cosponsor and never advanced past committee [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Government investigators keep the power to obtain phone and internet metadata with an administrative subpoena rather than a court warrant, and communications providers keep the existing compliance pathway; no one else is better off.

for.name: Rep. Ted Lieu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through introduction and committee referral; it advanced no further.

against.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: His committee never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, and it stalled at the subcommittee level.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken. The bill's only supporters were two House Democrats — Lieu and one cosponsor — and no Republican or Democratic leader ever acted for or against it on the record [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill removes their ability to demand customer metadata with an administrative subpoena, forcing them to persuade a judge instead. That convenience is precisely what the public privacy protection takes away.

industries.industry: Phone, email, and cloud service providers
industries.note: Providers would face a modest shift in how they process government requests — warrants instead of internal subpoenas for metadata — with little net burden since they already handle warrants for message contents. Their customers would gain the privacy protection.
